title: Shingon
hook: Kukai's esoteric school: mantra, mudra and mandala

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tendai, and Mount Hiei. Your line was the mother mountain. Which place that trained you came to mind? Today, a second Japanese school, on a different mountain. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-nine.

A young Japanese monk arrives at a temple in the Chinese capital, a long way from home. He's come to find a teacher. The master of the place is, the story says, not well. When the visitor is brought in, the old man smiles and says something like: I knew you were coming, and I've been waiting a long time. Then, instead of testing him for years, he begins handing over everything he knows. The visitor is Kukai. The story comes from Kukai's own report home. The teaching he carried back became a school. Today: Shingon.
screen: `A TEACHER WHO WAS WAITING.` → `EVERYTHING, HANDED OVER.` → `KUKAI CARRIES IT HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Shingon means true word, the Japanese rendering of mantra. We met Kukai on this path before, on the pilgrim's road and on his mountain, Koyasan. Today we open what he taught there. Second, the three mysteries. Shingon teaches through body, speech and mind together, and calls them the three mysteries. The body forms a mudra, a gesture of the hands. The speech recites a mantra, a sacred sound. The mind rests on a mandala, or on a single buddha pictured within it. In Shingon's teaching, these aren't three tricks for getting somewhere. They are the Buddha's own body, speech and mind, and the practitioner's body, speech and mind, meeting. Third, this very body. Kukai wrote an essay on becoming a buddha in this very body. Some Buddhists of his day spoke of awakening as the end of a road many lifetimes long. Kukai's claim was bolder: when the practitioner's gestures, words and thoughts are joined with the Buddha's, awakening is possible here, in this life, in this body. Fourth, why it's called esoteric. Esoteric means hidden, or inner. In Shingon, these practices are passed on from teacher to student, after the student has been prepared, the way the old master in China handed them to Kukai. So you'll hear Shingon described from the outside, as we're doing now, more than you'll see it explained in public. The hands, the sound and the mind are learned in person. What anyone can notice is the idea underneath: that body, speech and mind aren't obstacles to awakening. In Shingon, they're the doors.
screen: `SHINGON: TRUE WORD, MANTRA.` · `HAND, SOUND AND MIND TOGETHER.` · `A BUDDHA IN THIS VERY BODY.` · `PASSED ON FROM TEACHER TO STUDENT.` · then, large: `TRUE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one mudra. Nothing secret, just a simple gesture used in Buddhist meditation. Rest one hand in the other in your lap, palms up, and let the tips of the thumbs touch lightly, like they're holding a sheet of paper between them. Then sit. Keep the breath easy. Notice the hands. If the thumbs press hard, you're tense. If they drift apart, you're drifting. Let the gesture tell you how the mind is doing, and come back to it each time. The bell holds the time.
Shingon. True word: Kukai's esoteric school, joining mudra, mantra and mandala, body, speech and mind. Today's word.
Your line: true word. Today, pick one sentence you'll say to someone, and say it as if your hands, your voice and your mind all meant it at once. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Shingon Buddhists practice under a teacher, joining mudras of the hands, the recitation of mantras and meditation on mandalas; deeper practices are given only after initiation.

notes: Editor pass: removed 'old' for Kukai's teacher (an age claim not in the cited report).
The master's greeting is paraphrased ('something like') from Kukai's Shorai mokuroku; confirm the paraphrase and that Huiguo is described as unwell. Huiguo is not named in the voice.
'Some Buddhists of his day spoke of awakening as the end of a road many lifetimes long' is general framing for the contrast; confirm it is fair and does not rank schools.

The meditation gesture in the practice is described generically (one hand resting in the other, thumbs touching), without stating which hand is on top; Shingon and Zen forms differ. Confirm the description.
Avoids repeating year 3 day 927 (Koyasan), which covered the Shikoku pilgrimage and Kukai's eternal meditation.
Original: 真言, pronunciation SHIN-gohn; confirm.
